label: Bed and waking
rationale: Bedtime to morning: dreaming, waking, getting under the covers and setting the alarm, plus the kotatsu people crawl under on winter evenings.
mixUps: okiru from the versatility list gets mixed up with me ga sameru: okiru can mean getting out of bed, but me ga sameru never does. Getting into bed is going in, futon ni hairu, the same ni hairu as kotatsu ni hairu and ofuro ni hairu.

targets.trap: Not yume o motsu or yume ga aru, which mean having an ambition: dreams in your sleep are 'seen', yume o miru.
targets.use: Used for dreams in your sleep, usually in the past: hen na yume mita (I had a weird dream). A life ambition is yume ga aru instead.
targets.notes: Bedtime set phrase: oyasumi, ii yume mite ne (good night, sweet dreams).

example.english: I had a weird dream last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou hen na yume o mimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日変な夢を見ました。
examplePolite.english: I had a strange dream last night.

targets.english: wake up (from sleep); feel wide awake (me ga sameta)
targets.verbSense: wake, come out of sleep or a daze
targets.trap: English 'wake up' covers two things. okiru is waking or getting up (yonaka ni okichatta is fine), but me ga sameru is only the waking and never getting out of bed: yoji ni me ga sameta kedo, okita no wa shichiji.
targets.use: For the moment of waking, often unplanned: yonaka ni me ga sameta (I woke in the night). It also means feeling wide awake, e.g. after coffee. Getting out of bed is okiru.
targets.notes: Not the sameru of gohan ga sameru (food gets cold). mezamashi (alarm) comes from the transitive me o samasu (wake up, wake someone).

example.ja: 夜中に目が覚めちゃった。
example.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

examplePolite.romaji: yonaka ni me ga samete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 夜中に目が覚めてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

targets.english: get into bed, get under the covers
targets.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
targets.use: For getting under the covers, not necessarily asleep yet: mou futon haitta (I'm in bed now). Casual speech drops ni. futon also means the covers on a bed, so it's said with any bed; beddo ni hairu is also common.
targets.notes: Laying the futon out is futon o shiku; folding it away in the morning is futon o tatamu.

example.ja: もう布団入ったけど、眠れない。
example.english: I'm in bed, but I can't sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: futon ni haitte mo, nakanaka nemurenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 布団に入っても、なかなか眠れないんです。
examplePolite.english: Even after I get into bed, I can't get to sleep.

targets.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
targets.trap: English 'set' gives no hint of kakeru: alarms and timers take kakeru (araamu o setto suru is also fine).
targets.use: Said the night before, often as mezamashi kaketoku (I'll set the alarm). For phone alarms, araamu o kakeru and araamu o setto suru are just as common.
targets.notes: Shutting it off is mezamashi o tomeru; the alarm going off is mezamashi ga naru (mezamashi naranakatta = my alarm didn't go off).

example.ja: 明日早いから、目覚ましかけとく。
example.english: I'm up early tomorrow, so I'll set an alarm.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa hayai node, mezamashi o kakete okimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は早いので、目覚ましをかけておきます。
examplePolite.english: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'll set an alarm.

targets.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
targets.use: Winter at home: sitting with your legs under the heated table's quilt, often with mikan. Mostly heard as kotatsu haitte (get in) or kotatsu kara derarenai (I can't get out of the kotatsu).
targets.notes: Same hairu as futon ni hairu and ofuro ni hairu. Dozing off in it (kotatsu de neru) is the classic way to catch a cold.

example.ja: 寒い！早くこたつ入ろう。
example.english: It's freezing! Let's get under the kotatsu.

examplePolite.romaji: samui desu ne. hayaku kotatsu ni hairimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いですね。早くこたつに入りましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's cold. Let's get under the kotatsu.
